CausalChain: Intermittent fasting -> upregulation of tumor-suppressive miRNAs (e.g., miR-122) -> downregulation of glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PKM2) -> shift from aerobic glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation -> increased ROS production and apoptosis + reduced lactate-mediated immunosuppression -> enhanced sensitivity to targeted therapies
Hypothesis: Intermittent fasting induces upregulation of miR-122 in HCC cells, which suppresses key glycolytic enzymes, shifts metabolism towards oxidative phosphorylation, and thereby enhances pro-apoptotic ROS generation and reduces immunosuppression, ultimately improving the efficacy of targeted HCC therapies.
Abstract: Recent insights into the metabolic reprogramming of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have highlighted the central role of aerobic glycolysis in tumor progression and therapy resistance. Building on these insights, we propose that intermittent fasting may induce a metabolic switch in HCC cells via upregulation of tumor-suppressive microRNAs, notably miR-122. This upregulation could suppress key glycolytic enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2) and pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), thereby shifting cellular metabolism from a glycolysis‐dominated state to one reliant on oxidative phosphorylation. The consequent increase in mitochondrial activity is predicted to elevate reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, promote apoptosis, and reduce the immunosuppressive microenvironment fostered by lactate accumulation. This metabolic reprogramming, in combination with existing targeted therapies, may enhance treatment efficacy and overcome drug resistance in HCC.
